questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069068/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2st)=4st, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =2st.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(4st)(2t)+(-4)(2st) \\  & =8s{t}^{2}-8st \\  & =8st(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With Two Independent Variables
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069068/assets/21cec766fe72965697304ef4288ffb2b090ddfca179210165dbcfd42ec490b27.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{st})^{2}}=-{e}^{-2st}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\frac{1}{({e}^{-st})^{2}}=-{e}^{2st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =t{e}^{st}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =-t{e}^{-st}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s} \\  & =(-{e}^{-2st})(t{e}^{st})+(-{e}^{2st})(-t{e}^{-st}) \\  & =t{e}^{st}-t{e}^{-st} \\  & =t({e}^{st}-{e}^{-st}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Function of Three Intermediate Variables and Two Independent Variables
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069068/assets/b593a1b60fe8c1aef2c5c229ff426db350e6296b9ecb767494283f0fa3342072.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={e}^{x+y+z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={e}^{x+y+z}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={e}^{(s-t)+{t}^{2}+(s+t)}={e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & =-1, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & =2t, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂t} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot (-1)+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t+({e}^{2s+{t}^{2}})\cdot 1 \\  & =-{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}+{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t{e}^{2s+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069068/assets/be6afcdd0ad9ae0d7ef377c4918442a64e1186c90c25e27ec6c224d816a602fd.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y,z)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t),y=y(s,t)$ and $z=z(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂s}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x,y$ and $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂s} & =4s, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂s} & =1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂s} & =8s.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂s} & =(4)\cdot 4s+(3)\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 8s \\  & =16s+3-16s \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{x}^{6}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}(1+{x}^{4})}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{x\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}+\frac{3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}} \\  & =\frac{1+3{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$
